scope: Six general statements that complete the reviewed content for the twelve CMS pre-enrollment checklist topics (42 CFR 422.2274(c)(12) and 423.2274(c)(12)). Each is a general rule; none is a personal eligibility finding, date or amount for a specific person.

facts.title: Coverage outside the United States
facts.question: Does Medicare cover care outside the United States?
facts.text: Medicare usually does not cover health care outside the U.S., with a few narrow exceptions. Some Medigap policies cover emergency care during foreign travel, and some Medicare Advantage plans cover emergency care abroad. Medicare drug plans do not cover prescription drugs bought outside the U.S. Check the exact plan or policy before relying on it for travel.
facts.summary: Medicare usually does not cover care outside the U.S.; some Medigap policies and Medicare Advantage plans cover emergencies abroad.

facts.title: How a new plan affects the coverage you have now
facts.question: What happens to my current coverage if I join a new plan?
facts.text: When you join a new Medicare Advantage or Part D plan, your current plan ends when the new coverage starts. A Medigap policy cannot be used to pay Medicare Advantage copayments, deductibles or premiums. If you drop a Medigap policy you may not be able to get it back, because outside certain protected periods an insurer can ask health questions. Joining a plan can also end employer or retiree coverage for you and your dependents, so ask the benefits administrator before you enroll.
facts.summary: A new Medicare Advantage or Part D plan replaces the one you have; Medigap cannot pay Medicare Advantage costs and may be hard to get back.

sources.label: Medicare.gov: Medigap and Medicare Advantage Plans

facts.title: Plans change each year; the Evidence of Coverage
facts.question: Can a plan change, and where are its full rules?
facts.text: A plan’s premium, benefits, cost sharing, drug list and network can change each January 1. Each fall the plan sends an Annual Notice of Change listing what will change. The Evidence of Coverage is the plan’s full statement of what it covers, what you pay and its rules, including how to appeal.
facts.summary: Plans can change each January 1; the Annual Notice of Change lists changes and the Evidence of Coverage has the full rules.

facts.title: How to file a complaint
facts.question: How do I file a complaint about a plan?
facts.text: If you have a concern about a Medicare health or drug plan, you can file a complaint, also called a grievance. You can file it with the plan by following its membership materials, use the Medicare Complaint Form on Medicare.gov, or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). A complaint is different from an appeal, which asks a plan to reconsider a refusal to cover something.
facts.summary: A complaint (grievance) can be filed with the plan, through the Medicare Complaint Form, or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE.

facts.title: Who can join a Special Needs Plan
facts.question: Who can join a Special Needs Plan?
facts.text: Special Needs Plans are Medicare Advantage plans for people in specific situations. There are three kinds: for people who have both Medicare and Medicaid, for people with certain severe or chronic conditions, and for people who live in an institution or need that level of care. You can join one only if you meet its conditions, and you can stay enrolled only while you continue to meet them.
facts.summary: A Special Needs Plan is limited to people with both Medicare and Medicaid, certain chronic conditions, or institutional-level care needs.

facts.title: Your right to cancel an enrollment
facts.question: Can I cancel after I ask to enroll?
facts.text: You can cancel an enrollment request before the coverage starts by contacting the plan. Once coverage has started, leaving or switching plans is generally limited to Medicare’s enrollment periods.
facts.summary: An enrollment request can be cancelled before coverage starts; after that, changes follow Medicare’s enrollment periods.

sources.label: CMS Medicare Managed Care Manual, Chapter 2: cancellation of election
